extracted.intended_audience: public company executives, investor relations teams, compliance officers, general counsel, and boards of directors
extracted.subtask_short: Regulation FD compliance for public companies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and best practices for complying with Regulation Fair Disclosure (Regulation FD), including what counts as material nonpublic information, permitted dissemination channels, oversight responsibilities, and steps to avoid selective disclosures to analysts or shareholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on selective disclosure (Regulation FD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation FD prohibits public companies from selectively disclosing material nonpublic information (MNPI). It applies to statements made by, or attributable to, a company – including statements by members of the board of directors, senior management or those acting under their direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever a public company, or any person acting on its behalf, discloses MNPI to certain enumerated persons (e.g., securities analysts or institutional investors), the company must either (i) simultaneously (for intentional disclosures) or (ii) promptly (for non-intentional disclosures) disclose that same information to the general public. Violations can result in SEC enforcement actions, monetary penalties, or other relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality standard
rubrics_metrics.description: "Material" information is information such that there is a "substantial likelihood that a reasonable shareholder would consider it important" in making an investment decision or that it "would have been viewed by the reasonable investor as having significantly altered the 'total mix' of information made available."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materiality assessments must account for quantitative and qualitative factors, including expected market reaction. Subjective belief of provider or recipient that information is immaterial does not determine legal materiality — it is judged by an objective reasonable shareholder standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonpublic information definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is "nonpublic" if it has not been disseminated in a manner that would make it available to all investors generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For information to be public, it "must be disseminated in a manner calculated to reach the securities marketplace in general through recognized channels of distribution, and public investors must be afforded a reasonable waiting period to react to the information."

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognized channels of distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissemination through recognized channels may include press releases, filing a Form 8‑K that includes the information, publication on a company website (if that website is a recognized channel), or via social media (if the social media platform is viewed as a recognized channel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should identify which outlets are their recognized channels and use them for Regulation FD‑compliant disclosure. Social media can be acceptable if the company first takes steps to alert investors and the market to the channels it will use (see SEC guidance and the Netflix/Red Hastings example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated persons covered by Regulation FD
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule proscribes disclosures to (i) securities market professionals (brokers, dealers, investment advisers, institutional investment managers, sell‑side and buy‑side analysts) and (ii) shareholders, if it is reasonably foreseeable that they would trade on the basis of the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation FD is not a blanket prohibition on MNPI disclosures to everyone — it specifically targets selective disclosure to these enumerated groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing requirement for intentional vs unintentional disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: When MNPI is disclosed intentionally to an enumerated person, a company must disclose the same information simultaneously to the public. For non-intentional disclosures, the company must disclose the information promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should have procedures to effect timely public disclosures in the event of intentional or unintentional selective disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior management and board oversight duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior management and public company directors have fiduciary duties that include oversight of company policies protecting against breaches of federal securities laws and regulations, including Regulation FD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oversight responsibilities include ensuring that policies are in place, regularly reviewed, and enforced to prevent selective disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended components of Regulation FD protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Many public companies adopt Regulation FD protocols to strengthen compliance functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protocols typically establish procedures for earnings releases and contact with securities analysts; guidelines for monitoring postings on the company's website and social media; rules requiring prior approvals of speeches and interviews by senior management or directors; and processes for handling unintentional selective disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution around one‑on‑one calls with analysts and shareholders
rubrics_metrics.description: One‑on‑one calls with analysts and shareholders should merit particular caution under Regulation FD scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document what is communicated during private calls, consider ahead of any calls whether topics may constitute MNPI, and exercise care even if both parties believe information is not material — the SEC may find a violation based on objective materiality and context (e.g., timing before earnings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and recordkeeping of analyst outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracking analyst outreach (e.g., each analyst's original projection, who called them, adjustments after calls, internal meetings to discuss outreach) can demonstrate a pattern of selective disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While recordkeeping is good practice, detailed tracking that shows coordinated attempts to influence analyst estimates (as in the cited enforcement matter) can be used as evidence in enforcement actions; companies should document for compliance purposes but avoid conduct intended to steer estimates selectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of implied disclosures and signaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement actions have focused on selective communications that create 'implied disclosures' or signaling regarding earnings estimates, not only outright explicit MNPI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should be mindful that indirect guidance, signaling, or contextual timing (e.g., outreach immediately before earnings) can convey MNPI even if concrete data is not disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and timing as materiality‑amplifying factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Context and timing (for example, communications right before an earnings release) can make otherwise innocuous comments convey MNPI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even repetition of public information in a sensitive context can be treated as conveying MNPI; companies should consider timing when planning communications and analyst outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and enforcement posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of Regulation FD can result in SEC enforcement actions against companies and individuals, potentially leading to significant monetary penalties (e.g., the cited record $6.25 million penalty) and individual fines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SEC under current leadership is focused on curbing aggressive practices; settlements may be reached without admissions of wrongdoing, but penalties and public enforcement statements (quoting the Enforcement Division director) can signal enforcement priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices: training, policy review, and proactive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular training, policy reviews, and ongoing guidance regarding prohibited communications and disclosures are proactive and necessary steps to avoid Regulation FD violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying solely on self‑policing is risky; companies should provide periodic training, refresher sessions, and consider engaging compliance/legal teams to review analyst outreach and disclosure plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media disclosure requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media may be treated like a company website for Regulation FD purposes if it is one of the company's recognized channels of distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies must take steps sufficient to alert investors and the market to the social media channels they will use for dissemination (see SEC's guidance and the Netflix example). Failure to designate or alert investors to such channels may mean social media posts are not Regulation FD‑compliant.
